query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the relative content of oxidation‑prone elements (e.g., Al and Cr) in high‑entropy alloy protective coatings promotes the rapid formation of a dense, self‑lubricating oxide layer under high‑temperature wear conditions, thereby reducing both the friction coefficient and wear rate compared to a baseline composition.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‑entropy alloy coating with a standard composition (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi) that exhibits mixed wear mechanisms including abrasive, adhesive, and oxidative wear under high‑temperature conditions.
generation.intervention: Adjust the alloy composition by increasing the weight percentages of Al and Cr while keeping other elements constant, ensuring that the modification remains within processing and phase stability limits.
generation.conditions: Perform high‑temperature (approximately 800 °C) sliding wear tests in an oxidizing atmosphere (air) under controlled loading and strain rate conditions typical of aero‑engine or gas turbine applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, nanostructured protective oxide layer (such as Al2O3 and Cr2O3) at the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: Reactive wear protection: the in‑situ developed oxide scale acts as a barrier that minimizes direct metal‑to‑metal contact, thereby reducing both abrasive and adhesive wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coating, the modified coating with increased Al and Cr will have a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate. Surface analyses (via EDS/XPS) will reveal a thicker, more continuous oxide layer with higher oxygen content.
generation.baseline: High‑entropy alloy coating (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi) with standard levels of oxidation‑prone elements under identical wear test conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic effect should be observable under high‑temperature (650–1000 °C) oxidizing conditions. The hypothesis may not hold under low‑temperature or inert environments where oxide formation is minimal.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal increase in oxidation‑prone element content for maximum oxide layer efficacy and long‑term stability under cyclic wear remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high‑entropy alloy coatings: one with the baseline composition (standard AlCoCrFeNi) and one with increased Al and Cr levels. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests at 800 °C in air.
measurements: Conduct EDS and XPS analyses to assess surface oxide thickness and continuity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified coating does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate, or if surface analyses fail to show a substantially enhanced and continuous oxide layer compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAs protective coatings for the thermal parts of aero-engines, AlCoCrFeNi coatings have good application prospects. In this study, atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) was used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy coatings (HECs), which were oxidized from 650 °C to 1000 °C. The mechanism of the oxide layer formation and the internal phase transition were systematically investigated. The results show that a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure was formed at the initial stage of oxidation. The redistribution of elements and phase transition occurred in the HECs’ matrix; the BCC/B2 structure transformed to Al-Ni ordered B2 phase and Fe-Cr disordered A2 phase.Keywords: plasma spraying, oxidation behavior, high-entropy coatings, phase transition

High-entropy alloys (HEA) are a new type of advanced engineering alloy suggested by Yeh et al. and Cantor et al. in 2004 [,,,]. Unlike conventional alloys (e.g., nickel-based superalloys, stainless steels, etc.), HEAs are composed of more than five elements whose atoms are close to the iso-atomic ratio. They have high strength, good corrosion resistance, oxidation resistance and other properties at elevated temperatures. The reasons for the excellent performance of high-entropy alloys can be attributed to four major effects: thermodynamic high entropy, kinetic hysteresis diffusion, the organizational structure of the lattice distortion and the performance of the “cocktail” effect. High-entropy alloys have a high degree of structural complexity, and it is easy to form a single solid solution (single-phase FCC/BCC or two-phase FCC + BCC), which results in excellent mechanical properties. Coatings prepared from high-entropy alloys have the same excellent mechanical, high-temperature, wear-resistant and corrosion-resistant properties as thin films, and have broad application prospects in many fields. At present, great attention is being paid to this new alloy [,,,,,].
